title: Inference Compute in the Agent Era: Where the Money Flows for GPUs, HBM, and Compute Chips
excerpt: Agents are pushing AI chip competition from individual chips to entire systems. This article breaks down the profit sources across cloud platforms, data centers, GPUs, HBM, and advanced packaging based on a valid task, examines how contracts and financing amplify infrastructure build-outs, and evaluates edge AI as a secondary demand curve awaiting validation.
body: The operational mechanics of Agents are shifting the competitive landscape of AI chips from individual processors to entire systems. Agents plan steps, invoke tools, read results, and then resume inference. With every additional step, the model may need to reprocess context, read/write to the KV Cache, and consume compute, memory, and network resources. Therefore, compared to raw token consumption, what is currently more worth tracking is the **Effective Token Ratio** and the **inference invocation chain cost required per unit of paid value**. Agents will continue to drive up cloud-based inference demand, propagating this demand upstream along GPUs, HBM, advanced packaging, servers, networks, power supply, and liquid cooling. Profits will not be distributed evenly across all capacity expansion segments. The segments currently best positioned to command a premium are those that either control scarce capacity, yield rates, and customer certifications, or can integrate chips, software scheduling, and customer billing into a robust, deliverable system. Meanwhile, long-term contracts, prepayments, and debt financing transform future invocation expectations into today's data centers and equipment. Ultimately, should demand fall short of procurement assumptions, industry pressure will likely first manifest in utilization rates, lease pricing, and returns on assets. The edge constitutes a second demand curve. Automotive and smart home devices undeniably require lower latency, offline capabilities, and local data processing, yet this curve still requires validation in terms of usage frequency, device costs, and product gross margins. While the cloud has already entered a phase of massive construction, the edge is currently closer to a hypothesis awaiting proof from product behavior. ## Agents Turn Task Completion into a New Cost Unit Standard Q&A typically involves only a single round of input and output. Agents break an objective down into multiple steps, call external tools, retrieve results, and then determine the next move. A single task may encompass multiple rounds of model invocations, with different steps utilizing models of varying sizes. The number of invocations, context length, cache hit rates, and failure retries collectively dictate the final cost. Large Language Model (LLM) inference generally involves Prefill and Decode phases. Prefill processes the provided input and allows for substantial parallel computing. Decode generates new tokens sequentially, requiring repeated reading of model weights and the previously generated KV Cache, making it highly susceptible to memory bandwidth bottlenecks. As contexts lengthen, KV Cache consumption also scales with batch and sequence lengths. At this point, while peak compute remains important, memory capacity, bandwidth, cross-GPU communication, and scheduling efficiency will also directly constrain throughput. I use the following calculation to compare different inference systems. ```text Cost per Million Effective Tokens = Complete System Cost per Hour ÷ Effective Token Output per Hour × 1,000,000 ``` The complete system cost includes accelerators, HBM, servers, networking, power, liquid cooling, software, hosting, and depreciation. The effective token output per hour must be calculated based on a fixed model, average input/output lengths, concurrency, latency, and quality requirements. Queuing timeouts, failed retries, and results failing to meet quality standards should not be counted as output; input tokens, output tokens, and cache hits must also be logged separately. Only after unit task costs decrease can workloads—which previously could not cover the costs of model invocations, software integration, and human fallbacks—be viably incorporated into products. As prices drop further, usage may also rise. This growth has a clear prerequisite: task completion rates and the value of results must both meet expectations. Merely generating more tokens only inflates equipment utilization; it does not automatically translate into healthy demand. ## How an Agent Task Transmits to Infrastructure Profits A billable task first generates demand for model invocation and context processing, which subsequently translates into procurement for compute, memory, interconnects, and data centers. The diagram below consolidates demand transmission, the secondary curve of the edge, and financial risks into three layers. Reading from left to right, segments closer to the user more easily control scheduling and billing touchpoints, whereas segments further upstream rely more heavily on capacity, yield rates, and certifications to establish bargaining power. ```html ``` **GPUs, ASICs, and Software Stacks** The profit foundation for GPUs lies in their versatility, mature software ecosystems, and ability to quickly adapt to new models. While model architectures and request formats are still evolving, customers can use the same hardware and toolsets to handle training, development, and various inference tasks, keeping migration costs relatively manageable. ASICs can optimize cost and energy efficiency around fixed models, fixed precision, and stable request formats. Their economic viability requires three concurrent conditions: Workloads must reach sufficient scale; long-term utilization must cover chip R&D and deployment investments; and the software must seamlessly integrate the customer's existing models, operators, and operational workflows. For example, AWS packages Trainium with its Neuron software stack, servers, networking, and cloud services into a unified product, just as Google utilizes TPUs, interconnects, and Pathways to collectively support large-scale inference. These cases illustrate that the competitive unit for specialized chips has expanded to the entire system. Simply comparing the theoretical performance of an individual chip makes it difficult to judge whether it can generate sustainable profit. **HBM and Advanced Packaging** Long contexts and concurrent requests increase memory footprints for weights and KV Cache, while Decode requires continuous data movement. Consequently, HBM capacity and bandwidth directly impact accelerator utilization. Advanced packaging is responsible for integrating computing chips with multiple HBM modules, while also satisfying yield, power consumption, and customer certification requirements. During periods of short-term supply constraints, suppliers capable of reliably delivering qualified products are more likely to command a premium. Such premiums have clear conditions for retreat. As new capacity comes online, yields improve, alternative solutions pass certification, or customers begin diversifying their procurement, the bargaining power derived from supply tightness will weaken (for instance, with the emergence of companies similar to CXMT). As of September 2026, TSMC has revised its full-year capital expenditure guidance upward to $60–$64 billion, citing customer-driven capacity expansion as the primary driver. SK hynix disclosed that HBM4 began mass production and shipping in Q2 2026, with production volumes set to ramp up in the second half of the year; simultaneously, they have signed long-term agreements with roughly ten core customers. These corporate disclosures indicate that demand and capacity expansion are occurring concurrently, which is insufficient to prove that current premiums can be sustained long-term. **Servers, Networking, Power, and Liquid Cooling** GPUs and HBM must be installed in servers, connected to low-latency networks, and provisioned with stable power before they can constitute deployable computing power. Google provides Ironwood with a liquid-cooled configuration of up to 9,216 chips, where the total system power consumption approaches 10 MW. While this product specification does not represent all clusters, it highlights that procurement boundaries have extended well beyond the chip itself. Profits in these segments typically stem from power access, delivery speed, system integration, and reliability. They also bear **longer construction cycles** and heavier capital investments. Once data centers are built, depreciation, maintenance, and power contracts continue to incur costs. While revenue can grow rapidly alongside construction orders, capital returns depend on whether equipment is racked on schedule, whether utilization matches assumptions, and whether contracts can cover the asset recovery cycle. **Scheduling Software and Cloud Platforms** Cloud providers control customer gateways, model deployment, task routing, and billing. Scheduling software can enhance batch processing efficiency, reuse caches, and minimize idle time and failed retries, enabling the same hardware to execute more tasks. Cloud platforms can also distribute workloads between GPUs and proprietary ASICs, translating hardware cost variations into customer pricing or platform gross margins. This profit segment relies on customer usage scale, software compatibility, and migration costs, and is concurrently constrained by price competition and capital expenditures. Although cloud providers have purchased more equipment, their system advantages will only convert into sustainable returns once task revenues and cash flow catch up. ## Financing Causes Supply Construction to Precede Final Revenue AI infrastructure entails protracted procurement and construction cycles. Cloud providers plan computing capacity based on customer demand, GPU cloud service providers build data centers based on contracts, and server, memory, and packaging manufacturers expand capacity based on orders. Each node in the chain observes relatively early procurement signals; whether end-users will sustain their payments can often only be validated after the equipment is deployed. During TSMC’s Q2 2026 earnings call, management noted that while the individual demands presented by customers may be genuine, aggregating all demands still requires critical judgment. The company also monitors data center construction, locations, and racking progress to prevent chips from simply entering inventory post-delivery. This statement illustrates that upstream manufacturers are acutely aware of the gap between orders and final deployment. At the same time, Nvidia has partnered with financial institutions to package chips as financial assets for investing in small startups; while expanding its own sales volumes, it indirectly participates in frontier technology investments and establishes deep strategic lock-ins. According to their agreements and demand needs, these startups are required to continue purchasing chips from Nvidia in phases. Alternatively, Meta sets up shell companies to participate in data center construction; although this does not impact the parent company's financial statements on paper, such financial engineering could have highly destructive consequences amidst subsequent industry instability or volatility at other levels. While these phenomena do not definitively prove that a bubble has formed, they constantly reveal that current leverage is expanding aggressively. They demonstrate that long-term contracts and financing can front-load future revenue into today's servers, GPUs, and data centers. Provided that valid tasks continue to grow, advance construction can shorten delivery times and improve asset utilization. However, should demand growth, renewal rates, or utilization fall below procurement assumptions, lease, depreciation, power, and interest expenses will continue to accrue regardless. Consequently, industry stress will likely emerge first in asset returns. Even if total model invocations are still growing, as long as supply grows faster, GPU lease prices, used equipment residual values, server inventories, and certain memory prices will face downward pressure. Upstream suppliers may continue receiving orders before terminal demand actually slows, right up until a segment discovers that incremental revenue is insufficient to cover the cost of capital. At that point, the financial amplification process will transmit in reverse, triggering a bullwhip effect. ## The Edge is a Secondary Curve Awaiting Validation from Usage Behavior Automotive assistants and smart home control hubs demand rapid response times and must execute partial operations even under weak network conditions. Furthermore, in-car environments, home sensors, and personal habits involve privacy concerns, meaning local processing can reduce the volume of data uploaded. Edge environments are well-suited for wake-up, perception, simple decision-making, and high-frequency control, whereas complex inference and long contexts can still be offloaded to the cloud. Local execution consumes the power of user devices, yet device manufacturers must still bear the upfront investments. Higher-spec SoCs, memory, and storage inflate the BOM (Bill of Materials), while thermal management, model adaptation, security, OTA updates, and multi-year post-sales support also demand significant engineering resources. Manufacturers are only justified in sustaining these costs long-term if local inference can support higher price points, reduce cloud invocation expenditures, improve user experiences, or satisfy privacy and offline requirements. Edge chips must also process model updates within constrained power budgets. Low-bit quantization, more efficient memory architectures, and edge-cloud orchestration can mitigate these limits; however, the mere capability to deploy does not equate to stable demand. True usage frequencies of automotive and smart home devices, local execution ratios, incremental hardware costs, and product gross margins remain the most critical validation metrics for this curve. Once edge AI permeates high-frequency devices, demand will become more fragmented and align more closely with genuine daily user behavior. Current public materials remain insufficient to prove that this stage has arrived; therefore, I retain it as a secondary curve and refrain from preemptively translating product demos into massive chip orders. ## Signals I Will Monitor Cloud demand hinges on paid task volumes, task completion rates, and unit task revenue. While Effective Tokens can facilitate comparisons across inference systems, they must be contextualized alongside latency, quality, and failure rates. Cloud providers' capital expenditures must also translate into AI cloud service revenues, cash flows, and higher output per megawatt. In the supply chain, one must monitor whether HBM and standard DRAM prices and inventories are diverging, whether advanced packaging delivery cycles are shortening, and whether GPU lease prices and secondary residual values are beginning to decline. Profits derived from tight supply will only approach durable advantages if yield rates, certification moats, and customer stickiness can be maintained post-expansion. Regarding financial structures, one must observe whether contract terms, debt maturities, and the economic lifespans of GPUs align. Customer renewals, data center racking progress, and utilization rates will help determine whether long-term contracts are locking in genuine demand, or merely pricing future demand into today's investments. On the edge, key metrics include the daily average usage of assistants, local completion ratios, and device gross margins. Only after automotive and smart home devices begin managing high-frequency tasks will the demand for edge chips transition from a spec-sheet competition into product capabilities that users are willing to utilize continuously. If valid tasks and revenues can keep pace with compute supply, there remains room for expansion in GPUs, ASICs, HBM, packaging, and data centers. Profits will increasingly concentrate in segments capable of reducing unit task costs, commanding constrained supply, or controlling customer and scheduling gateways. If utilization, renewals, and asset returns consistently trail procurement assumptions, even if the Agent narrative remains valid, expectations for this current wave of infrastructure investment will need to be downgraded. ## Key Sources - [NVIDIA Inference Optimization Guide](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/mastering-llm-techniques-inference-optimization/), Prefill, Decode, KV Cache, and memory bandwidth - [AWS Trainium Official Documentation](https://aws.amazon.com/ai/machine-learning/trainium/), system design encompassing the chip, Neuron software stack, servers, networking, and cloud services - [Google Ironwood Official Overview](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/infrastructure-and-cloud/google-cloud/ironwood-tpu-age-of-inference/), compute, memory, interconnects, and liquid cooling configurations for large-scale inference - [TSMC Q2 2026 Earnings Call](https://investor.tsmc.com/chinese/encrypt/files/encrypt_file/reports/2026-07/547d1696765e05ce3adb81c108ce1c8c1682b80c/TSMC+2Q26+Transcript.pdf), capital expenditures, capacity expansion judgments, and terminal deployment verification - [SK hynix Q2 2026 Business Results](https://news.skhynix.com/en/q2-2026-business-results), HBM4 shipments, long-term agreements, and capacity expansion plans
